title: Dynamic typing versus C# and TypeScript static types
hook: JavaScript variables hold any value at run time — types are discovered when code executes. C# and TypeScript check types before run time, but only TypeScript disappears at run time.

blocks.text: **Dynamic typing** means a variable's type is determined by the value it currently holds, and can change on reassignment. `let x = 42; x = 'hello';` is legal JavaScript. **Static typing** (C#, TypeScript) assigns a fixed type at compile time — changing from `number` to `string` is a compile error. TypeScript is a **structural** static type system: it checks shapes at build time, then **erases** all type annotations — the run time is plain JavaScript. C# types survive compilation into Intermediate Language (IL) and are enforced by the Common Language Runtime (CLR) at run time.

entries.plainDefinition: Types belong to values, not variable declarations. Checked at run time with typeof, instanceof, or by trying operations.
entries.example: `let data = fetchResult;` — data could be anything.

entries.plainDefinition: Types are known at compile time. Compiler rejects incompatible operations before the program runs.
TypeScript removes type annotations during compilation. No run-time type information remains.
If it walks and quacks like a duck, treat it as a duck — behavior matters, not declared class.
entries.example: `obj.map(fn)` works if `.map` exists, regardless of `instanceof Array`.

blocks.text: Dynamic typing enables rapid prototyping but pushes type errors to production unless you add tests or TypeScript. A C# API controller with `int studentId` fails at build if you pass a string. The same bug in JavaScript surfaces as `NaN` or a silent wrong query. TypeScript bridges the gap: you get compile-time checks without changing the run time. Understanding that TS types vanish explains why `JSON.parse` returns `any` and why you still need run-time validation at system boundaries.

blocks.title: Three-way comparison
blocks.body: JavaScript: dynamic at run time. C#: static at compile and run time (CLR). TypeScript: static at compile time only — run time is JavaScript.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: JavaScript — run time only
items.body: No compile step for types. Errors appear when code runs: `TypeError`, `NaN`, wrong branch taken.

items.title: C# — compile time + run time
items.body: Compiler checks types. CLR verifies on cast (`InvalidCastException`). Reflection can inspect types at run time.

items.title: TypeScript — compile time only
items.body: tsc checks types, then strips them. Output .js has no type info. Use Zod/io-ts at boundaries for run-time safety.

items.title: Gradual typing with JSDoc
items.body: TypeScript can check plain .js files via `// @ts-check` and JSDoc `@param` annotations — optional static layer.

snippet.label: Dynamic typing in JavaScript
snippet.explanation: Lines 1–5: one variable, two types over its lifetime. Lines 7–13: functions accept any type — behavior depends on caller. This flexibility is the core tradeoff of dynamic typing.

snippet.label: TypeScript catches errors at compile time
snippet.explanation: Lines 2–3: static type on variable. Lines 5–8: parameter and return types enforced at build. Lines 10–12: emitted JavaScript has no trace of types — run-time is identical to untyped JS.

snippet.label: C# static typing equivalent
snippet.explanation: Lines 2–3: compile-time rejection. Lines 5–6: parameter types enforced at compile. Lines 8–9: `object` box survives to run time — cast fails at CLR with exception. C# types are not erased.

snippet.label: Run-time validation at system boundaries
snippet.explanation: Lines 1–3: JSON.parse returns untyped data — TS types cannot protect here. Lines 6–16: manual or library validation at the boundary. Production pattern: validate external input regardless of TypeScript.

blocks.title: Dynamic vs static across the stack
Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Assuming TypeScript protects run time — it does not. Skipping validation on `JSON.parse` results because 'we use TypeScript'. Confusing C# `dynamic` (run-time binding via DLR) with JavaScript's default behavior. Thinking `var` in C# is like JavaScript dynamic typing — C# `var` is compile-time inference.

blocks.text: JavaScript is dynamically typed and duck-typed: `Array.isArray` aside, behavior follows available properties. TypeScript adds a structural type system — `{ x: number }` is compatible with any object with `x: number`, not a specific class. C# defaults to nominal typing (class names matter) though generics and interfaces add flexibility. C# `dynamic` uses the Dynamic Language Runtime (DLR) for late binding — closer to JS than to `var`. TypeScript `any` disables checking; `unknown` forces narrowing (like a safer `object`). At FAANG interviews, articulate the boundary pattern: static types inside your codebase, run-time schemas (Zod, protobuf, JSON Schema) at edges. typeof null bug and coercion exist because JS has no compile-time type enforcement.

blocks.title: Tradeoffs at senior level
rows: Catch bugs early, great IDE support
Not the same as TS — types survive

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Claiming TypeScript adds run-time type checks. Saying C# var is dynamically typed. Not validating external input because TS compiles. Confusing structural typing with duck typing without explaining the difference.

interviewTakeaways: JavaScript types are checked at run time; variables can hold any value.
TypeScript checks at compile time then erases types — run time is plain JS.
C# enforces types at compile time AND run time via CLR — types are not erased.
Always validate JSON.parse and external API data at run time regardless of TS.
60s: JS dynamic run time. TS static compile only, erased. C# static compile+runtime. Validate boundaries.
commonPitfalls: Weak: 'TypeScript makes JavaScript type-safe.' Strong: 'TS is compile-time only; validate at boundaries.'
Assuming C# var is dynamic — it is compile-time inference.
Strong answer: 'Dynamic JS at runtime. TS erased. C# CLR enforces. Zod/schema at API edges.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: TS matches shapes, not class names. Use `unknown` instead of `any` for untrusted data, then narrow with typeof/is.
C# `var` infers static type at compile time. `dynamic` defers to DLR at run time — different from JS default and from TS.
